pedagogy.summary: At 8-9, using structure becomes a deliberate calculating tool: breaking 7×13 into 7×10 + 7×3 with the distributive property, using place value to explain why ×10 shifts every digit one place left (not 'add a zero'), and using the quadrilateral hierarchy (a square is a special rectangle) to carry properties down from category to subcategory. The teaching aim is that the child looks for a known structure before grinding a procedure. The area model is the workhorse: it makes the distributive split visible as two sub-rectangles, and CCSS MP7 names exactly this partitioning as the heart of the practice.
bestPractices: Model 7×13 on a partitioned area rectangle (7×10 and 7×3) so the split is seen, then connect it to the numeric decomposition
Teach ×10 as a place-value shift using a place-value chart (digits move one column left; a zero fills the emptied ones place) rather than the 'add a zero' rule, which breaks for decimals
Use overlapping property sets / a shape family tree so squares sit inside rectangles inside parallelograms, and reason 'a square must have… because it is a rectangle'
Prompt 'is there a number fact or shape fact you already know that this is like?' before any standard algorithm
keyRepresentations: Partitioned area model / grid for the distributive split
Place-value chart showing digits shifting left on ×10/×100
Shape hierarchy diagram (quadrilateral → parallelogram → rectangle → square)
Arrays and factor trees linking multiplication structure
commonMisconceptions: Uses 'multiplying by 10 adds a zero', which fails for decimals (2.5×10 read as 2.50)
Splits distributively but forgets to multiply the second part (7×13 = 7×10 + 3)
Refuses that a square is a rectangle because the names/looks differ, so properties don't transfer down the hierarchy
Treats each multiplication as needing the column algorithm, not looking for a decomposition that makes it easy

learn.summary: For ages 8-9, this topic develops the habit of looking for known mathematical structure before grinding a procedure: splitting a multiplication like 7×13 into 7×10 + 7×3 (distributive property), explaining ×10 as a place-value shift (digits move one column left) rather than 'add a zero', and using the quadrilateral hierarchy (a square is a special rectangle) to inherit properties from category to subcategory. The partitioned area model is the central representation, making the distributive split visible as two sub-rectangles. Activities centre on learners partitioning, justifying and generalising the structural move, not just reaching a correct answer.

activities.title: Split the rectangle: 7×13 from two easy facts
feedback: If a learner writes 7×10 + 3 = 73, point back to the rectangle: the second part is also 7 tall, so it is 7×3 = 21, not 3. Have them shade the missing 7×3 block.
If a learner reaches 91 only by the column algorithm, ask them to show the two sub-rectangles and name the two easy facts, so the structure is made explicit.
When a learner tries a second valid split (e.g. 11 and 2) and still gets 91, confirm that any split works because the ×7 is shared over the parts — the choice is just about which parts are easiest.
activities.rationale: The area model makes the distributive partition literally visible as two sub-rectangles and ties the picture to the numeric decomposition. CCSS MP7 gives this kind of distributive split (e.g. 7 × 8 = 7 × 5 + 7 × 3) as one example of 'using structure', alongside other examples. An interactive version where the learner drags the divider and watches the parts recompute and slide together is one proposed way to make the mechanism operate under the learner's hand, and a drawn, cut or folded paper rectangle may serve the same purpose; the relative effectiveness of either medium is not established by the cited sources. An array alongside the area model (the original row's arrays/factor-trees representation) could optionally reinforce the same structure.
sourceClaims: Using structure includes partitioning a product distributively (e.g. 7×8 = 7×5 + 7×3) as the basis of the distributive property
Teaching should help pupils recognise and use mathematical structure and relationships, choosing representations (e.g. area models, place-value charts) that expose structure and are gradually removed
learnerActions: Face 7×13 drawn as a rectangle 7 tall and 13 wide; mark where to cut the width to make a friendly 10 and 3
Cut the rectangle into a 7×10 part and a 7×3 part and work out each: 70 and 21
Combine the two parts (70 + 21 = 91) and state the matching number sentence: 7×13 = 7×10 + 7×3
Explain in your own words why BOTH parts have to be multiplied by 7 (both sub-rectangles are 7 tall)
Try a different cut of 13 (for example 11 and 2, giving 7×11 = 77 and 7×2 = 14) and check you still reach 91; say which cut was easiest and why
activities.intendedInsight: A multiplication that feels hard can be assembled from two multiplications you already know; the distributive property shares the ×7 across every part of the 13, which is why both parts must be multiplied.

activities.title: Why ×10 shifts digits, not 'adds a zero'
feedback: If a learner writes 2.5×10 = 2.50, show the chart: 2.50 is the same value as 2.5, so nothing has changed — ×10 must make it ten times bigger, which means shifting to 25.
Reinforce that for 36×10 = 360 the zero appears because the ones column is emptied, not because we 'add a zero' as a rule.
activities.rationale: A place-value chart exposes the structural reason behind the ×10 pattern and provides a built-in counterexample (the decimal case) to the shortcut. A live chart where digits slide one column on ×10/×100 can make the shift concrete, and a paper chart with movable digit cards can serve the same purpose; the relative effectiveness of the media is not established by the cited sources.
sourceClaims: Teaching should help pupils recognise and use mathematical structure and relationships, choosing representations (e.g. area models, place-value charts) that expose structure and are gradually removed
learnerActions: Place a number such as 36 in a place-value chart (tens and ones), then multiply by 10 and move each digit one column to the left, writing a 0 in the emptied ones place to read 360
Now push 2.5 through ×10 in the same chart: move each digit one column left to get 25, and notice that appending a zero would wrongly give 2.50 (the same value as 2.5)
State a rule in your own words: ×10 moves every digit one place left; 'add a zero' only looks right for whole numbers because a zero happens to fill the empty ones place
Repeat for ×100 (two columns left) with one whole number and one decimal
activities.intendedInsight: Multiplying by 10 (or 100) is a place-value shift of every digit; 'add a zero' is only a lucky special case for whole numbers and breaks for decimals.

activities.title: Nested shape families: a square is a special rectangle
feedback: If a learner denies that a square is a rectangle, use the nested sets: the square sits inside the rectangle set, so it must satisfy every rectangle property (four right angles).
If a learner claims every rectangle is a square, show a long thin rectangle as a counterexample — inheritance runs from the wider category to the narrower one, not back up.
activities.rationale: A shape family tree / nested property sets make the hierarchy visible and are intended to support reasoning by inheritance, which is the structural move for quadrilateral classification. Tappable property labels on a hierarchy diagram can serve as a reference; a sort by itself checks or teaches classification but does not itself elicit the learner's explanation, so pair the active sorting with a request to justify. The attached EEF claim supports using representations to expose structure in general and does not specifically evidence the nested-set method.
sourceClaims: Teaching should help pupils recognise and use mathematical structure and relationships, choosing representations (e.g. area models, place-value charts) that expose structure and are gradually removed
learnerActions: Sort a set of quadrilaterals into nested property sets so squares sit inside rectangles, which sit inside parallelograms
For a given square, list what must be true of it just because it is a rectangle (e.g. it has four right angles) — without measuring
Complete sentences of the form 'A square must have … because it is a rectangle' and 'A square must have … because it is a parallelogram'
Decide and justify: is every rectangle a square? Explain why the inheritance runs one way down the hierarchy
activities.intendedInsight: Subcategories inherit the properties of the categories that contain them, so knowing 'a square is a rectangle' lets you carry rectangle properties down without re-checking; but the reverse is not guaranteed.

activities.title: 'What do I already know that this is like?' — probing and generalising
feedback: Listen for a structurally justified decomposition such as '7×13 is 7×10 plus 7×3, that's 70 and 21, so 91 — I can split the 13 because multiplying is shared out over the parts.' The justification, not the answer 91, is the target.
If the learner reaches 91 only by running the column algorithm in their head, that does not yet show structural insight — ask them to name the parts and why the split is valid.
If the learner cannot say why the split works, return to the area model activity before pushing generalisation.
activities.rationale: The answer 91 is reachable by the column algorithm with no structural insight; what discriminates is whether the learner decomposes and can justify the split, and whether they transfer the move to related products. Open probes are intended to elicit the justification that a scored answer would hide.
sourceClaims: Using structure includes partitioning a product distributively (e.g. 7×8 = 7×5 + 7×3) as the basis of the distributive property
learnerActions: Work out 7×13 mentally using a fact you already know instead of the written column method, then talk through how you split it and why that split is allowed
Answer: could you have split 13 a different way and still got 91? Which split was easiest and why?
Generalise: how is splitting 7×13 like splitting 6×13 or 7×23? Describe the structural move you reused
Before any standard algorithm on a new product, pause and ask 'is there a number fact or shape fact I already know that this is like?'
activities.intendedInsight: Using structure is a deliberate, transferable habit: decompose into known parts and justify the decomposition, rather than defaulting to a procedure.

constraints: The teaching aim is that the learner looks for a known structure before applying a standard procedure; reaching the correct numerical answer by the column algorithm does not demonstrate this objective.
Target the justification, not just the result: a distributive split must be explained as sharing the ×7 over both parts, and ×10 must be explained as a place-value shift.

Tap-to-reveal annotations on a pre-split area model or a shape hierarchy are useful as reference scaffolds, but they do not let the learner choose the split point or watch the parts recombine; use them to support, not replace, active partitioning.

Recognition or matching checks (e.g. 'which split makes 7×13 easy?') can confirm the structural move, but a correct selection can hide the reasoning; pair any such check with a request to explain why.
Avoid teaching 'multiply by 10 adds a zero' as a rule; use it only as a named special case for whole numbers alongside the place-value explanation.
Inheritance in the quadrilateral hierarchy runs from broader to narrower categories (a square inherits rectangle properties), not the reverse; make this directionality explicit.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and medium/interaction choices are presented with proposed/may wording.

The legacy row rated dialogue ('conversation') and 3D as 'poor' with claims such as 'dialogue without the area model gives nothing to partition' and '3D adds load, not insight'. These comparative/necessity claims are not established by the cited sources and have been reframed as narrow scaffold limits rather than universal laws; the open probes retained here use discussion productively once a visual model is available.

The original keyRepresentation 'arrays and factor trees linking multiplication structure' was not carried into any activity as a standalone task; it is noted as an optional reinforcement in activity 1 and could be reinstated to enrich the distributive-split work. Flagged as a substantive representation gap rather than silently dropped.

The EEF source claim is a general representation/structure statement; attaching it to the shape-hierarchy activity supports the 'use a representation to expose structure' principle but does not specifically evidence the nested-property-set approach — treated as topical support, not validation.

Self-audit of arithmetic: 7×13 = 7×10 + 7×3 = 70 + 21 = 91 (correct); alternative split 7×11 + 7×2 = 77 + 14 = 91 (correct). The common error 7×10 + 3 = 73 is retained only as an explicitly labelled misconception with a correction, never as a valid answer. 2.5×10 = 25 (correct); 2.50 is flagged as the wrong 'add a zero' outcome. 36×10 = 360, 6×13 = 78 and 7×23 = 161 by the same method (used only as generalisation prompts, not as stated answers).

probeDeeper: Ask 'you split 13 into 10 and 3 — could you have split it a different way and still got 91? which split was easiest and why?' to test flexible, purposeful structure use
Counterexample tuned to this topic: 'does "add a zero" give the right answer for 2.5×10? why or why not?' to check the place-value structure beneath the rule
Ask 'a square is a rectangle — so what does that let you say about its angles without measuring?' to probe property inheritance in the hierarchy
Ask 'how is splitting 7×13 like splitting 6×13 or 7×23?' to see whether the distributive structure generalises
assess.correctAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for a distributive decomposition justified structurally: '7×13 is 7×10 plus 7×3, that's 70 and 21, so 91 — I can split the 13 because multiplying is sharing out over the parts.' The justification, not the 91, is the target.

errorPatterns.pattern: Splits distributively but multiplies only the first part, giving 7×10 + 3 = 73, because the split is treated as chopping the number rather than sharing the ×7 over both parts
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to the area model: both sub-rectangles are 7 tall, so the 3 must also be multiplied by 7; see the missing 7×3 block
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child says '70 plus 3' or otherwise leaves the second part un-multiplied

errorPatterns.pattern: Relies on 'multiplying by 10 just adds a zero', which misfires on decimals and hides the place-value shift
errorPatterns.nextMove: Use a place-value chart to shift every digit one column left; contrast the whole-number case where a zero happens to fill the ones place
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Asked to explain ×10 or to do 2.5×10, the child appends a zero (2.50) instead of shifting digits

errorPatterns.pattern: Refuses that a square is a special rectangle, so shared properties don't transfer down the hierarchy
errorPatterns.nextMove: Sort quadrilaterals into nested property sets so the square sits inside the rectangle set; reason that a square inherits rectangle properties
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Asked 'is a square a rectangle? so must it have four right angles?' the child denies the category link

responseLevels.gap: Reaches for the column algorithm or splits incorrectly (7×10+3), appends a zero for ×10, and won't accept the square-rectangle link
responseLevels.full: Chooses a distributive decomposition unprompted and justifies it via the area model, explains ×10 as a place-value shift, and reasons about inherited quadrilateral properties — applying 'what do I already know that this is like?' to new products and shapes
responseLevels.partial: Can carry out a distributive split or state a hierarchy fact when prompted, but cannot justify why the split is valid or transfers 'add a zero' unsafely to decimals

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Work out 7 × 13 in your head, using a fact you already know instead of the written column method. Talk me through how you split it up and why that's allowed.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The answer 91 can be reached by the column algorithm with no structural insight. What discriminates is whether the child DECOMPOSES and can say why the split is valid. A child using structure partitions and justifies; a child without it either runs the algorithm mentally or splits wrongly (7×10+3).
